outcome: Since 26 January 2024 no event I found bears on whether every integer is a sum of four integer cubes. The residue class n ≡ ±4 (mod 9) is still listed as unproven in every source I could read (Wikipedia's revision of 15 January 2026 says 18x±4 and 18x±5 remain unproven). The in-window items found concern prime cubes, polynomial cubes or sums of three cubes, and are recorded as discounted neighbours.
problem_asks: (1) For every integer n, positive, negative or zero. (2) Whether n can be written as x³ + y³ + z³ + w³ with x, y, z, w integers, negative cubes allowed (the Wikipedia article says the cubes may be negative, unlike Waring's problem). This is one yes/no existence claim quantified over all integers. 'Perfect cubes' is read as cubes of integers, as the article reads it. Not asked by the bullet: how many representations there are (the infinitely-many conjecture is background, not the bullet), the natural-number or positive-cube version (a different problem), or the sums-of-three-cubes question.

events.what_happened: W. Sierpiński and A. Schinzel, 'Sur les sommes de quatre cubes', Acta Arithmetica vol. 4, no. 1. Wikipedia dates it 1959; a Cambridge reference list (search excerpt) gives the same volume and pages as 1958, so the year is unsettled. The paper proves that every integer in the residue classes 0 and 3 (mod 6) and 1, 7, 8 (mod 18) is a sum of four integer cubes; replacing x by −x gives the opposite classes. Together these cover every integer except those ≡ ±2, ±4, ±5 (mod 18). It also gives explicit decompositions for |n| ≤ 300 except ±148, ±257, ±284. I did not open the paper; the content is from Wikipedia's account and a search excerpt.
events.delivers: Affirmative for the named residue classes with signed cubes: every integer ≡ 0 or 3 (mod 6), and every integer ≡ ±1, ±7, ±8 (mod 18). Restricted to those classes; silent on the rest.
events.remains: Every integer ≡ ±2, ±4 or ±5 (mod 18). Demjanenko's 1966 identities (next event) take the ±2 (mod 18) part; what remains after both is ≡ ±4 (mod 9), written by Wikipedia as 18x±4 and 18x±5.

checked_by.qualification: Peer-reviewed number theory journal of record
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper. I did not read it, so no checking beyond publication is established.

events.directly_checkable: The residue-class identities and the decompositions for |n| ≤ 300 are explicit and can be checked by expanding the four cubes. I did not check any of them.
events.direction: Affirmative for the residue classes it covers. No counterexample.
events.object: Explicit identities expressing each integer in the listed residue classes as a sum of four integer cubes (constructive identities, not an existence proof), plus a table of explicit decompositions for |n| ≤ 300 except ±148, ±257, ±284.

events.what_happened: V. A. Demjanenko (also spelled Dem'yanenko), 'Sums of four cubes', Izvestiya Vysshikh Uchebnykh Zavedenii. Matematika vol. 54, no. 5 (1966), pp. 63–69 per Wikipedia. The mathnet.ru record (ivm2756) surfaced in search; the page refused my connection, so I did not open it. Per Wikipedia: identities for the 18x±2 case; the 108x±38 exceptions handled by more advanced methods, completing 18x±2; and decompositions for many numbers in the 9x±4 case, extended to |n| ≤ 1000. A Warwick lecture deck by Visser (PDF returned binary, so I saw only a search excerpt) states the result as: for k ≢ ±4 (mod 9) there are infinitely many integer solutions to w³ + x³ + y³ + z³ = k, and lists identities for 6n, 6n+3, 18n+1, 18n+7, 18n+8, 54n+2, 54n+20, 216n−16, 216n+92, and a Pell-equation family for 108n+38.
events.delivers: Every integer not ≡ ±4 (mod 9) is a sum of four integer cubes, in infinitely many ways (Visser's slide excerpt; consistent with Wikipedia's statement that only the 9x±4 case remains). For the ±4 (mod 9) class it gives explicit decompositions for many numbers with |n| ≤ 1000 (Wikipedia). Signed cubes.
events.remains: Every integer ≡ ±4 (mod 9), i.e. 9x±4. Wikipedia says these are unproven. The 1966 coverage there is explicit decompositions to |n| ≤ 1000, not a proof for the class.

events.directly_checkable: The identities are explicit polynomial identities that can be checked by expanding the four cubes. The slide excerpt lists them, but I did not check any.
events.direction: Affirmative for every residue class except ±4 (mod 9). No counterexample.
events.object: Explicit identities expressing n as a sum of four integer cubes for each listed residue family (6n, 6n+3, 18n+1, 18n+7, 18n+8, 54n+2, 54n+20, 216n−16, 216n+92). The 108n+38 family is given by an identity for 108(83ℓ+i)+38, i = 0,…,82, built from solutions of a Pell equation (a² − 3420b² = 1, per the slide excerpt). Constructive, not existence-only.

events.what_happened: Philippe Revoy, 'Sur les sommes de quatre cubes', L'Enseignement Mathématique t. 29 (1983), pp. 209–220. Wikipedia's text dates Revoy's report to 1982 and its reference to 1983. Cited as reporting that the four-cube question is neither proven nor disproven. I did not read the paper; the only content I have is the citation and that status statement.
events.delivers: Status statement only, as far as my sources show: the signed four-cube question is open. No result identified.
events.direction: Consistent with the problem being open. No counterexample.

events.what_happened: Henri Cohen, 2004, as cited by Wikipedia: a simpler summary of the earlier identities, and a statement that the four-cube question is neither proven nor disproven. Wikipedia cites a paper archived from Cohen's website. I could not locate it, so the characterisation is Wikipedia's alone.
events.delivers: No new result as far as my sources show. Restates earlier identities and reports the problem open. Discounted.
events.doubts: I could not locate the paper, so I cannot say whether it contains any new content beyond restating Demjanenko's identities. 'No engagement' here means none found in my searches.
events.direction: Consistent with the problem being open. No counterexample.

events.what_happened: Koichi Kawada, 'On the sum of four cubes', Mathematika vol. 43, no. 2 (1996), pp. 323–348 (published online 26 February 2010, DOI 10.1112/S0025579300011815). The opened extract frames the Waring-type conjecture that every sufficiently large natural number is a sum of four cubes of natural numbers, and writes it as E(N) ≪ 1, where E(N) counts the natural numbers up to N that are not such sums. The extract does not state the paper's own results.
events.revisions: Journal print date 1996; the online publication date is 26 February 2010.
events.delivers: Could not determine from the extract. The framed question is the natural-number (positive-cube) Waring version, a different question from signed integer cubes.
events.remains: The signed-integer problem, which the extract does not address.
events.doubts: I read only the extract, so I cannot say what the paper proves.
events.direction: Not determined from my reading. The question it frames is the natural-number version, so it does not cut either way on the signed problem.

events.what_happened: Siu-lun Alan Lee, 'On Waring's problem: two cubes and two minicubes', arXiv:1006.5142 (math.NT), posted June 2010. Abstract (from search excerpt; I did not fetch the full text): almost every positive integer is a sum of four positive cubes, two of which are at most n^θ, for θ ≥ 192/869; an asymptotic count is given for 1/4 < θ < 1/3. Brüdern's 2012 Acta Arithmetica paper discusses it (search excerpt only).
events.delivers: Almost every positive integer (not every integer), with positive cubes, two of them restricted in size. A different question from every integer as signed cubes.
events.remains: Every integer, with signed cubes, including the exceptional set for the signed problem.

checked_by.qualification: Analytic number theorist working on Waring-type problems
checked_by.what_they_did: Discusses Lee's theorem and sharpens a lower bound in Acta Arithmetica 2012, according to a search excerpt. I did not read it.
checked_by.where: Acta Arithmetica 2012 (citation from search excerpt; not opened)

events.direction: Almost-all result for positive cubes. Does not touch the claim for every integer. No counterexample.

events.what_happened: Jörg Brüdern and Trevor Wooley, 'On Waring's problem: three cubes and a minicube', Nagoya Mathematical Journal vol. 200 (2010), pp. 59–91. Per search excerpts (not opened): almost every natural number is a sum of four positive cubes, one of them at most n^{5/36}; Theorem 1.1 gives r_θ(n) ≥ 1 for almost all n when θ ≥ 5/36. Davenport (1939) first showed that almost all natural numbers are sums of four positive cubes.
events.revisions: The journal year is 2010. I did not establish when the first preprint appeared.
events.delivers: Almost all natural numbers, with positive cubes and one cube bounded. A different question from every integer as signed cubes.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper. I did not read it.

events.direction: Almost-all result for positive cubes. No counterexample; does not address every integer.

events.what_happened: J.-M. Deshouillers, F. Hennecart and B. Landreau, with an appendix by I. Gusti Putu Purnaba, Mathematics of Computation vol. 69 (2000), pp. 421–439. Per a search excerpt of the AMS abstract (the AMS page refused my fetch): 'We conjecture that 7,373,170,279,850 is the largest integer which cannot be expressed as the sum of four nonnegative integral cubes.' OEIS A022566 lists the 113,936,676 such non-representable integers under the nonnegative convention. Zimmermann's records page repeats the bound as 'every integer greater than 7,373,170,279,850 is a sum of 4 cubes', without stating a sign convention, and credits the group with a five-cube result to 10^16. The OEIS treats the threshold as a conjecture.
events.delivers: A conjecture about nonnegative cubes: that a finite set of exceptions ends at 7,373,170,279,850. Nothing proved about signed cubes. The five-cube result is a different problem.
events.remains: The signed four-cube problem for every integer, including the nonnegative-cube conjecture's own exception set if the signed problem is read in its nonnegative form.
events.directly_checkable: The nonnegative exception set is a finite list that can be checked by computation. I did not check it.
events.doubts: The threshold is stated as a conjecture by its authors and by the OEIS. The sign convention matters: the bullet asks about signed cubes, but the threshold is stated for nonnegative cubes, while Zimmermann's line omits the sign. I found no verification of the threshold in my searches.
events.direction: A conjecture about nonnegative cubes. Consistent with the signed problem, but not a result on it.

events.what_happened: Zimmermann's records page on cubes (undated) states: 'we have first computed all sums of 2, 3 and 4 cubes less than 10^9', giving counts of 440959 sums of two cubes, 100735175 of three and 966039273 of four. The same page attributes a five-cube exhaustive search (1290741 to 3375000000000) to 'In collaboration with Olivier Ramaré and Francois Bertault', with a Math. Comp. 68 (1999) reference. The page does not say whether the four-cube table is part of that work or of another, or whether the four-cube sums are signed or nonnegative.
events.revisions: The page is undated. The five-cube result it describes is attributed to Math. Comp. 1999.
events.delivers: A finite computation: all four-cube sums below 10^9 tabulated. Finitely many integers, so it does not move the universal claim.
events.remains: Every integer beyond 10^9, and the whole universal claim.
events.directly_checkable: The table is a finite computation; the Hugging Face dataset below gives certificates to 10^9 that anyone can check row by row.
events.doubts: The page is undated and does not give the authors of the four-cube table or the sign convention, so I cannot tie it to a publication.
events.direction: Consistent with the affirmative conjecture on the range checked. No counterexample found below 10^9.

events.what_happened: Hugging Face dataset 'sum4cubes' under account kzoacn (licence CC-BY-4.0). The card gives explicit certificates x1³ + x2³ + x3³ + x4³ = n for every 0 ≤ n ≤ 1,000,000,000, in 100 shards (56.9 GB). The card says the generator uses a 'congruence-filtered generalized Pell search' and that each identity is checked with exact integer arithmetic before it is written. The card does not state a creation date.
events.revisions: No creation date on the card, so I could not place it before or after 26 January 2024.
events.delivers: Finite: signed four-cube representations for every n ≤ 10^9. It shows every integer in that range is representable, and it does not move the universal claim.
events.remains: Every integer beyond 10^9, and the whole universal claim.

events.what_happened: Tak-Wing Ching and K. M. Tsang, 'Waring–Goldbach problem involving cubes of primes', Mathematische Zeitschrift (2020), pp. 1–13 (per the HKU faculty page, search excerpt). They prove that at least 8.25% of the positive integers in certain residue classes satisfying the necessary conditions are sums of four prime cubes, improving Ren's 1.5% and Liu's 2.911%. The restatement is Theorem 1.1 of Zhai's arXiv:2201.07346, which I opened.
events.delivers: A lower density bound for sums of four prime cubes in restricted residue classes. About primes, not integer cubes. A different problem.
events.remains: The sums-of-four-integer-cubes problem for every integer.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper. I did not read it.

events.doubts: A search summary described the 8.25% figure as a result about integers. The restatement in arXiv:2201.07346 is explicitly about sums of four prime cubes, so I have recorded it as a prime-cube result.
events.direction: Affirmative for prime cubes in restricted residue classes. Not about integer cubes. No counterexample.

events.what_happened: Zhichun Zhai, 'Problems related to Waring-Goldbach problem involving cubes of primes', arXiv:2201.07346, submitted 3 January 2022 (one version). The abstract studies whether certain integers are sums of four prime cubes, and raises open problems. The comments state: 'No rigorous proof was provided. Some problems were raised.' It restates the Ching–Tsang result in Theorem 1.1.
events.delivers: Nothing new on integer cubes. Restates a prime-cube density bound and raises questions. Discounted as a neighbouring problem.
events.remains: The sums-of-four-integer-cubes problem for every integer.
events.doubts: The author's own comments say no rigorous proof is given.
events.direction: Does not cut on the integer-cube problem. About primes.

events.what_happened: Christian Elsholtz and Jan-Christoph Schlage-Puchta, 'The density of integers representable as the sum of four prime cubes', arXiv:1902.09858 (math.NT), submitted 26 February 2019 (one version). The exact sentence: 'The set of integers which can be written as the sum of four prime cubes has lower density at least 0.009664.' It improves earlier bounds of 0.003125 (Ren) and 0.005776 (Liu).
events.delivers: A lower density bound for integers that are sums of four prime cubes. About primes, not integer cubes. A different problem.
events.remains: The sums-of-four-integer-cubes problem for every integer.
events.direction: Density bound for prime-cube sums. Does not cut on integer cubes.

events.what_happened: Ajai Choudhry, 'Expressing an integer as a sum of cubes of polynomials', arXiv:2311.07325 (math.NT), submitted 13 November 2023 (one version). Abstract: infinitely many integers are sums of four cubes of polynomials with integer coefficients; identities express 1 and 2 this way; every integer is a sum of five cubes of such polynomials. I read the abstract only.
events.delivers: Infinitely many integers as sums of four cubes of integer-coefficient polynomials. A polynomial analogue, not integer cubes, and not every integer. Discounted.
events.remains: Every integer as a sum of four integer cubes.
events.directly_checkable: The identities for 1 and 2 are explicit and checkable by expansion. I did not check them.
events.direction: An analogue (polynomial cubes). Does not cut on the integer-cube problem.
events.object: Explicit identities expressing 1 and 2 as sums of four cubes of integer-coefficient polynomials, per the abstract. Not checked by me.

events.what_happened: Kenny Applegate and Kyle Pratt, 'Computational results on sums of a prime with squares or cubes', arXiv:2609.20505, submitted 17 September 2026 (one version). They conjecture every integer above 14 is an odd prime plus two positive squares, verify this up to 10^26, and show that integers 308 to 10^16 are sums of an odd prime and two positive cubes. The method uses integral points on elliptic curves. The paper names no AI tool.
events.delivers: Sums of an odd prime and two positive cubes, and a conjecture about prime plus two squares. Not four cubes of integers. Discounted as a neighbouring problem.
events.remains: The sums-of-four-integer-cubes problem for every integer.
events.direction: Does not cut on the four-cube problem. Not about four integer cubes.

events.what_happened: Narinder Kumar Wadhawan and Priyanka Wadhawan, 'Representation of integers by sum of three cubes, a new approach based on seed equation', arXiv:2512.15763, submitted 12 December 2025 (one version). The abstract is about sums of three cubes. It mentions no sums of four cubes, no four-cube conjecture, and no ±4 (mod 9) class.
events.delivers: Sums of three cubes via seed equations. A neighbouring problem. Nothing on four cubes. Discounted.
events.remains: The four-cube problem for every integer.
events.direction: Does not cut on the four-cube problem.

disputes.summary: The 7,373,170,279,850 threshold is stated for nonnegative cubes in the 2000 abstract and in OEIS A022566, but Zimmermann's records page states it for 'sums of 4 cubes' with no sign convention, and the bullet asks about signed cubes. I have not resolved which convention the threshold is meant in beyond what the abstract says.

Sources disagree on dates: Sierpiński–Schinzel 1959 (Wikipedia) versus 1958 (a Cambridge reference list, same volume and pages); Revoy 1982 (Wikipedia text) versus 1983 (Wikipedia reference and HandWiki). The 8.25% prime-cube figure was reported in one search summary as an integer result; the arXiv restatement shows it is for prime cubes.

summary: The Wikipedia article (revision of 15 January 2026, read through a condensed fetch) still lists the signed four-cube problem as conjectured affirmative but neither proven nor disproven, and says the 18x±4 and 18x±5 cases, i.e. the class n ≡ ±4 (mod 9), remain unproven. The classical results were all found and recorded as events: Sierpiński and Schinzel covered several residue classes (1959); Demjanenko covered the rest outside ±4 mod 9 (1966, per Wikipedia and a Warwick slide excerpt, neither of which I could read in full); Revoy (1983) and Cohen (2004) are status statements. The class ±4 mod 9 is the only one without a proof, and this is also the reason four cubes is the minimum: such integers are not sums of three cubes, since cubes are 0 or ±1 mod 9. The 1966 coverage for that class is explicit decompositions up to |n| ≤ 1000 per Wikipedia, and a 2020s Hugging Face dataset gives explicit signed certificates for every n ≤ 10^9. Under §2.1 these are finite instances of a universal claim and do not move the problem. No in-window event on signed four cubes was found. The in-window items I opened (Applegate–Pratt 2026 on prime-plus-cubes; Wadhawan 2025 on three cubes) are discounted neighbours. Close calls: (i) whether the 1966 identities cover every class outside ±4 mod 9 depends on Wikipedia and a slide excerpt, because the 1966 text was not readable here; (ii) whether the finite 10^9 tables and the |n| ≤ 1000 decompositions should count as movement is a judgement left to the pass, and I recorded them as events so it can be made; (iii) the 7,373,170,279,850 nonnegative-cube threshold is a different convention from the bullet, so I recorded it and discounted it for the signed problem, though a reader who takes 'perfect cubes' to mean nonnegative cubes would weigh it differently. AI search: no source I read names an AI system for this problem. I searched for AI involvement across lab announcements, benchmarks and tracker-type sources. OpenAI's Astra announcement (1 August 2026, ten results) was read through secondary reports only, because the OpenAI page refused my fetch; the reports I could read list no cubes result. AlphaProof Nexus (arXiv:2605.22763, 9 Erdős problems and 44 OEIS conjectures) was read at abstract level; its per-item list was not read. OEIS Open (arXiv:2608.11941) names no system for this problem and does not mention cubes. Epoch's FrontierMath Open Problems lists a sum-of-three-cubes item for 114 as open as of July 2026, which is a different problem and not an event here. A June 2025 Goodreads post saying 'no one knows' was read as a search excerpt and is weak status evidence only.
competing_reading: Read 'perfect cubes' as nonnegative cubes, as in Waring's problem. Then the live question is the 2000 conjecture that 7,373,170,279,850 is the largest integer that is not a sum of four nonnegative cubes (OEIS A022566), and the relevant events are Deshouillers–Hennecart–Landreau 2000, Kawada 1996 and Brüdern–Wooley 2010, with a different residue-class story. Nothing in-window moves that either. Conversely, a reader who sees Demjanenko's coverage of every class except ±4 mod 9 and the explicit decompositions up to 1000 for that class might call the bullet nearly settled. The article's own status sentence, and the lack of any proof for 9x±4, say it is open.
what_would_settle_it: (a) A proof, or a counterexample, for an integer ≡ ±4 (mod 9); (b) the texts of Demjanenko 1966 and Sierpiński–Schinzel 1959, to confirm exactly which classes and what 9x±4 coverage they give; (c) a dated arXiv or journal item after 26 January 2024 on four signed cubes (none found, but I could not run arXiv full-text search directly); (d) the OpenAI 'Ten advances' page and its openai/ten-proofs repository, the AlphaProof Nexus per-item results, and the OEIS Open list, checked for any four-cube item, in particular A022566; (e) the Wikipedia article's history after 15 January 2026.
